name: Lobes of the Cerebral Cortex
what: This subtopic covers the four lobes of the cerebral cortex, their internal regions, and the specific roles of each in behaviour and mental processes. The frontal lobe handles motor movement and executive functions; the parietal lobe processes touch and body sensation; the occipital lobe processes vision; and the temporal lobe processes sound and language.
why: The lobes and their specific regions provide a precise anatomical framework for understanding localisation of function. This knowledge is directly applied in clinical diagnosis, in interpreting neuroimaging findings, and in evaluating case studies of brain injury.

items.title: I can describe the role of the prefrontal cortex in executive functions
items.what: The prefrontal cortex is an association area in the frontal lobe responsible for executive functions, including logic, reasoning, judgement, decision-making, planning, problem-solving, personality, and the expression and regulation of emotions. It reaches full maturity at around 25 years of age.
items.why: The prefrontal cortex is the anatomical basis for the most distinctly human cognitive capacities. Its late maturation explains adolescent impulsivity and is relevant to legal and educational contexts.
items.example: The case of Phineas Gage illustrates the prefrontal cortex's role in personality. Before his accident, Gage was calm and reliable. After a metal rod destroyed parts of his prefrontal cortex, he became impulsive and unreliable, demonstrating that this region underlies personality and social behaviour.

items.title: I can describe the sequence of motor processing across the prefrontal cortex, premotor cortex, and primary motor cortex
items.what: Voluntary movement involves three frontal lobe regions in sequence. The prefrontal cortex recognises that a movement is needed and plans it. The premotor cortex organises this into a fluid sequence of motions. The primary motor cortex then signals the cerebellum to relay these instructions to the skeletal muscles.
items.why: Understanding this sequence clarifies that voluntary movement is not a single brain event but a coordinated multi-stage process. It also explains why damage to each region produces a distinct type of motor impairment.
items.example: To pick up a glass of water: the prefrontal cortex registers the goal of picking it up, the premotor cortex sequences the reach-grasp-lift movements, and the primary motor cortex sends the final commands to the arm and hand muscles via the cerebellum.

items.title: I can explain the role of Broca's area in speech production
items.what: Broca's area is an association area located only in the left frontal lobe. It is responsible for the production of fluent speech by coordinating the muscle movements required for speech, including tongue, lip, jaw, and vocal cord movements.
items.why: Broca's area is a classic example of localisation of function and hemispheric specialisation. Damage to it causes Broca's aphasia, in which a person can understand language but cannot produce fluent speech.
items.example: A patient with damage to Broca's area following a stroke can understand instructions and knows what they want to say, but produces only slow, effortful, telegraphic speech such as 'want...water' instead of 'Can I please have a glass of water.'

items.title: I can describe the role of the primary somatosensory cortex and explain its proportional organisation
items.what: The primary somatosensory cortex is a sensory area in the parietal lobe that receives and processes touch, temperature, pressure, and pain. The amount of cortex devoted to each body part is proportional to the density of sensory neurons in that part, not to its physical size.
items.why: This proportional organisation explains why some body regions, such as the lips and fingertips, are far more sensitive than others. It also informs the interpretation of the sensory homunculus as a tool for understanding cortical representation.
items.example: The fingertips have a very high density of sensory receptors and occupy a disproportionately large region of the primary somatosensory cortex. This is why a person can distinguish two pencil points 2 mm apart on their fingertip but may not detect the same separation on their back.

items.title: I can describe the role of the primary visual cortex and the occipital lobe's association area
items.what: The primary visual cortex is a sensory area in the occipital lobe that receives and processes visual information sent from the retina via the optic nerve. The association area of the occipital lobe then integrates this raw visual information with details from memory to enable meaningful perception and interpretation.
items.why: The distinction between receiving visual data and interpreting it as meaningful objects or scenes helps explain conditions such as visual agnosia, where a person can see but cannot recognise objects.
items.example: If a person sees a round red object, the primary visual cortex processes the raw visual data, colour, shape, and edges. The association area then integrates this with stored memories to identify the object as an apple.

items.title: I can describe the roles of the primary auditory cortex and Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
items.what: The primary auditory cortex receives and processes auditory information. The left hemisphere's auditory cortex processes verbal sounds such as speech, while the right processes non-verbal sounds such as music. Wernicke's area, located only in the left temporal lobe, is responsible for comprehending speech and producing meaningful, coherent language.
items.why: These two areas together handle the full cycle of language comprehension. Understanding their distinct roles explains why some patients lose comprehension but not production, or vice versa, depending on which area is damaged.
items.example: A patient with damage to Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe can speak fluently and with normal rhythm, but their speech is filled with made-up words and does not make sense. They also cannot understand what is said to them, because comprehension is impaired.

items.title: I can compare Broca's area and Wernicke's area in terms of their similarities and differences
items.what: Both Broca's area and Wernicke's area are association areas located only in the left cerebral hemisphere, and both are involved in language. However, Broca's area is in the frontal lobe and is responsible for speech production, while Wernicke's area is in the temporal lobe and is responsible for speech comprehension and the production of meaningful content.
items.why: Distinguishing these two areas is frequently tested and clinically important. Confusing production and comprehension is a common error when interpreting aphasia cases.
items.example: Both a patient with Broca's aphasia and one with Wernicke's aphasia have language impairments. The Broca's patient struggles to speak but understands what is said to them. The Wernicke's patient speaks easily but produces meaningless speech and cannot understand others.

items.title: I can explain contralateral functioning of the primary motor cortex, primary somatosensory cortex, and primary visual cortex
items.what: The primary motor cortex, primary somatosensory cortex, and primary visual cortex all function contralaterally, meaning each hemisphere controls or processes input from the opposite side of the body or visual field. For example, the left primary motor cortex initiates movement on the right side of the body.
items.why: Contralateral functioning explains the predictable pattern in which strokes or injuries to one hemisphere produce deficits on the opposite side of the body, a fact with major clinical diagnostic significance.
items.example: A patient who suffers a stroke in the right hemisphere experiences weakness and sensory loss on the left side of their body, because the right primary motor cortex and right primary somatosensory cortex control the left side of the body.
